children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

Twenty-five years ago today, the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks shook America to its core. The conventional wisdom is that 9/11 changed everything. Longtime Journal editor John Bussey, who was at Ground Zero when the first plane hit near the Journal's downtown office at the time, argues that's true, but with a caveat. His essay examines how the decisions America made after 9/11, along with the interventions it didn't make, helped shape the world we live in today.

We also scoured hundreds of articles from our archives to show you how Sept. 11 altered American politics, the economy and the national psyche, and how its effects continue to reverberate. And in a special video, Journal staffers who covered 9/11 recount the events of that day and how our newsroom reported the attacks as they unfolded.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES

The second night of the GOP midterm convention featured a fiery, future-looking speech from JD Vance and poignant tributes marking the anniversary of Charlie Kirk's assassination and the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
President Trump has promised every adult citizen a $5,000 "Trump Dividend." Here's what to know.
In Iran, the economic fallout from the war and the U.S. blockade is adding to the pain facing ordinary citizens already struggling with a plunging currency, worsening joblessness and rising prices.
Cryptocurrency billionaire Fred Ehrsam, a Trump administration ally and co-founder of Coinbase, has emerged as a surprise contender in Trump's push to revitalize Venezuela's run-down oil industry.
Chinese biotech companies are training their sights on one of the most lucrative medicines: GLP-1s.
America's fast-food chains are boosting employee training and prioritizing customer service after finding that digital kiosks and apps turned off some diners.
3. LIVE FROM THE MARKETS
Follow our live financial coverage all day.
A monthslong selloff in government bonds is skidding into dangerous ground, pushing borrowing costs toward levels that some fear will finally damage the stock market and the economy.
The Pentagon is in talks to lend roughly $5 billion to AI cloud-computing startup Fluidstack, which would mark by far the Office of Strategic Capital's largest loan to date.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Congress is suddenly waking up to the AI doomsday threat.

After years of limited action, dozens of lawmakers are touting new proposals to regulate artificial-intelligence models that have stepped up their capabilities. The bipartisan concerns ratcheted up after a departing Anthropic researcher warned that the lab and its competitors are building systems they won't be able to control. Lawmakers are now calling for everything from a new federal regulatory agency and AI "kill switches" to a ban on superintelligence. But there's little indication a gridlocked Congress will turn the flurry of regulatory talk into law, report Amrith Ramkumar and Yoko Kubota.
This simple hack could help you score a lower mortgage rate.

For years, government-backed mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac relied exclusively on classic FICO scores to evaluate creditworthiness and set mortgage rates. That just changed. Lenders are now free to also pull VantageScore 4.0, an alternative scoring model that makes some borrowers look more creditworthy, and use the score that results in the best rate. That could be especially valuable now that the 30-year fixed mortgage rate has topped 7% for the first time in more than a year. Veronica Dagher explains why asking your lender to pull both could potentially save you thousands of dollars.

6. SEE THE STORY
See inside the homes college athletes are buying with their NIL money.

Buying a house used to be a crowning achievement after an athlete turned pro. Now, college football players earning hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars a year are jumping into the real-estate market. Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita traded student housing with five roommates for a $950,000 four-bedroom house with mountain views and a pool. Other players are buying million-dollar homes, renting rooms to teammates and building real-estate portfolios. Take a look inside the homes where college athletes are putting their newfound wealth to work.

U.S. Open men's singles semifinals.
Economic Data: The Labor Department releases the August consumer-price index.
Earnings: Kroger, Rent the Runway
Today's paper
8. THE NUMBER
$100 million

That's the size of the gift billionaire investor Stuart Zimmer and his wife pledged to Harvard in 2018, before he stopped funding it after the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel. Now, after roughly two years of courtship by Harvard President Alan Garber, Zimmer has resumed funding the gift, offering a glimpse of the delicate line universities are walking with mega-donors who pulled back their giving over schools' responses to the attacks.
9. AND FINALLY...
Does your Uber really need 30 air fresheners?

Getting into an (Uber) or (Lyft) has become an assault on the nostrils. Drivers pack their cars with scented trees, puck-shaped cans that hide under seats and vent clips that blow fragrance into riders' faces. Some passengers are calling for fragrance-free cars, but drivers say they're just trying to keep their cars smelling good between riders. After all, passengers emit all kinds of smells from the back seat. "Sometimes people fart," one driver said.
10. BEYOND THE NEWSROOM
Opinion: The U.S. has prevented, or deterred, another 9/11. The question is whether we have the fortitude and tools to prevent the next attack.
